Designing with Carran-carramulk

A unit at the place now called Dights Falls, on Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung Country. It begins with where you stand and ends with a design brief written with Country. Select a lesson on the river to open it.

This is Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung Country. Sovereignty was never ceded. Cultural authority for Carran-carramulk sits with Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung people.

Lesson 1 · Listen

Where do I stand?

Interactive timelineExit ticket
Learning intention
Develop a better understanding of my own relationship to place and Country, and gain insight into the layered colonial and First Nations history of Carran-carramulk (Dights Falls).
Success criteria
  • I can describe a place I am connected to, what it provides me, and what I give back.
  • I can recall at least one Wurundjeri and one colonial layer of history.

Part 1: Map a place you are connected to

Choose a place that matters to you: a park, a street, a kitchen, a beach, a court. Show it in any mode: drawing, writing, photo or voice memo.

  1. The place I am connected to is…
  2. It gives me…
  3. What I give back to it is…
  4. If it changed or disappeared, I would feel…

Part 2: The layers of Carran-carramulk

Read the history of the rock bar as layers. Each was laid over the one before, but none erased the place underneath. Audio narration for each layer is on the class page.

About the name

Carran-carramulk is a Woiwurrung name recorded for this stretch of river and the area now called Abbotsford. Published sources say carran means prickly myrtle. This meaning comes from secondary sources, so we use the name with care and check it with Wurundjeri people. Birrarung is the river's name, recorded as meaning "river of mists". "Dights Falls" comes from John Dight's 1841 flour mill.

Who is speaking?
Layer 1 · Deep time to now

The rock bar and the river

Before any weir, this was a natural place of meeting, crossing and fishing. These uses never stopped belonging to the place.

  1. Lava meets old rock

    The river narrows here, squeezed between basalt from a lava flow about 800,000 years old and a much older spur of sedimentary rock. The cliff opposite still shows the layers.

    c. 800,000 years agoWikipedia

  2. Where salt water meets fresh

    Below the rock bar the river is tidal. Above it, the water stays fresh. The falls are a threshold between two kinds of water.

    Melbourne Water

  3. A crossing place and a fish trap

    Woi wurrung people from north of the river and Boon wurrung people from the south used the falls as a crossing point and a place to catch migrating fish. Eels (iuk) and other fish moved up the river past the natural rocks to breed.

    Old Treasury Building · Wurundjeri-approved

  4. A meeting place for clans

    The junction of Merri Creek and the Birrarung was an important meeting place for trade, marriage, settling disputes and ceremony. In January 1844 the Wurundjeri-willam hosted a very large gathering of people from across central Victoria.

    Walking MapsWikipedia

  5. Wurundjeri, the Manna Gum people

    The name Wurundjeri joins wurun, the manna gum common along the Birrarung, and djeri, a grub found in or near the tree. People and plants are named together.

    Victorian Collections · citing Wurundjeri Corporation

Stop and think

STARTName two reasons people gathered here.

GO FURTHERWhy would a narrow part of a river be a good meeting place? Think like a designer about how land shapes movement.

Layer 2 · 1803 to 1851

The colonial line

Settlers arrived, built a weir across the rock bar and set up government stations nearby. The place became what historians call a "contact zone".

  1. A boat party reaches the falls

    A survey party led by Charles Grimes rowed up the river and reached the falls on 8 February 1803. A marker above the falls calls them the first white men to "discover" the river. People had lived with this river for tens of thousands of years.

    1803Wikipedia

  2. The first weir and the Ceres mill

    John Dight bought the land in 1838. With his brother Charles he built a weir above the falls to power the Ceres flour mill, finished in 1841. The weir became a barrier for the fish that had moved past the rocks for generations.

    1838–1841eMelbourne

  3. The Protectorate and the Native Police

    Assistant Protector William Thomas was based close to the falls from 1843 to 1847. The Native Police Corps was stationed nearby in 1843–44. These were government attempts to control Aboriginal people's lives on their own Country.

    1843–1847eMelbourne

  4. The Merri Creek Aboriginal School

    Just upstream, the Merri Creek Aboriginal School ran from 1845 to 1851, supported by the ngurungaeta (clan head) Billibellary. Wurundjeri people today trace their ancestry to students of this school. The school, Protectorate and burial sites are listed as one of the most significant post-contact Aboriginal places in Melbourne.

    1845–1851eMelbourneHeritage Victoria

Stop and think

STARTThe weir is a straight line across moving water. What did it add, and what did it take away?

GO FURTHERRead the 1803 entry again. Whose story does the word "discover" tell, and whose does it leave out?

Layer 3 · 1890s to 1970s

Concrete and freeway

More infrastructure was built over the place. Some of it covered the earlier layers completely.

  1. A licensed weir and a water scheme

    In 1891 the Melbourne Flour Milling Company was licensed to build and maintain a weir here. Water from the falls also supplied the Royal Botanic Gardens from the 1890s to the 1930s. Milling here seems to have ended by 1909.

    1891–1930sWeekend NotesWikipedia

  2. Yarra Bend Park

    Land to the east became Yarra Bend Park in 1933. For most of the 20th century the falls themselves were hard for the public to reach.

    1933eMelbourne

  3. The Eastern Freeway

    Building the Eastern Freeway, finished in 1972, changed the course of the river and destroyed the Deep Rock Basin. The freeway and a bike path now pass over the sites of the school and Protectorate.

    1970seMelbourneHeritage Victoria

Stop and think

STARTFind one thing in this layer that covered up something older.

GO FURTHERWhere can you see a straight line laid across the fluid lines of the river?

Layer 4 · Now

Repair, care and continuing connection

Some recent work tries to undo damage. Wurundjeri people continue to gather here and care for Country.

  1. The fishway

    A vertical-slot fishway was built beside the weir in 2012 so that fish such as the threatened Australian grayling and the short-finned eel can move upstream again.

    2012Arthur Rylah Institute

  2. Replanting the creek

    Groups such as the Merri Creek Management Committee and Friends of Merri Creek replant local species including red gum, manna gum, black wattle and murnong (yam daisy). The Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung Narrap team helps manage land along the Merri.

    Merri Creek Management Committee

  3. A living place

    The Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung Education Unit runs cultural walks from Abbotsford Convent to Dights Falls. Wurundjeri educators share stories of their connection to the falls and their responsibility to heal Country.

    TodayWurundjeri Woi-wurrung Education Unit

Stop and think

STARTIs the fishway a fix, or a patch on a bigger problem? Give a reason.

GO FURTHERPress "Settler records". How much of this history comes from settler institutions? What does that tell you about where we need to listen next?

Exit ticket

One thing I aim to document on our excursion is…

It can be literal, such as an object, a piece of architecture or a plant or animal. It can also be abstract, such as change or dislocation.

Supports

  • Choose your own mode for Part 1.
  • Use the larger-text button and the audio narration.
  • Sentence starters above support EAL/D students.

Lesson 2 · Listen

Walking Carran-carramulk

Excursion
Learning intention
Observe, record and feel Country through attentive, respectful looking and listening.
Success criteria
  • I can gather at least five observations across drawing, photography and writing.
  • I can follow site protocols.

On arrival

We begin with an Acknowledgement of Country, ideally led by a Wurundjeri guide from the Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung Education Unit. Listen first. Pencils and phones down.

Site protocols

  • Walk slowly and stay with your group.
  • Only record what you are told you can record. No photos of people or ceremony without permission.
  • Nothing leaves Country: no rocks, plants, bark or feathers.

Prompt cards

Take a card at each stop. Gather at least five observations in total, using at least two of drawing, photography and writing.

Sense

Stand still for one minute. What can you hear, smell and feel? Which sounds are human and which are not?

Signs of change

Find something that has been added, removed, repaired or worn away. Who or what changed it?

Landmarks in context

At the weir, the fishway and the Merri Creek junction, recall what you learned in Lesson 1. What layer are you looking at?

Your exit-ticket focus

Look for the thing you said you would document in Lesson 1. Record it at least once.

Choose your way of walking

  • Guided: use the icon-based prompt cards in order.
  • Wander: if you work well independently, roam within the agreed area and set your own prompts.
  • Record in any medium. If the freeway noise is too much, tell your teacher and use ear protection or a quieter spot.

If you can't attend

Use the teacher's field audio, photo set and the class Padlet. Complete the same prompts from those. Your observations count equally.

Lesson 3 · Notice

The shared archive

Milestone 1: field observations30-minute digital lessonPadlet
Learning intentions
Curate our collected material to see how we see Country, and see what is lost when we describe and visualise a place rather than experience it directly.
Success criteria
  • I can upload and caption two or three pieces on the class Padlet.
  • I can respond meaningfully to a peer's post.
  • I can name one limit of describing Country through a digital archive.

Open the Carran-carramulk Padlet

Our archive isn't organised as a map with coordinates. It's organised by experience. Each section of the Padlet is a way of meeting Carran-carramulk, and you choose where your piece belongs.

Steps

  1. Choose a section

    Look through the sections and choose the one that best fits what you experienced. If none of them fits, add a new section with your own heading. That counts as a contribution too.

  2. Upload and caption

    Add two or three pieces from the walk: a drawing, photo, piece of writing or voice note.

    Caption frame: What: This is… Where: I found it at… What I noticed: I noticed…

  3. Respond to a peer

    Comment on one classmate's post: "I notice… I wonder…"

  4. Spot a cluster or a gap

    Which sections filled up quickly? Which stayed empty? What did nobody record, and why might that be?

  5. Closing reflection

    Post one sentence to the Padlet: what does our archive show about Carran-carramulk, and what does it leave out? If there's no section for this yet, start one called "What the archive can't hold".

Supports

  • Record an audio caption instead of typing.
  • Use the caption frame above.
  • If you couldn't attend the walk, post from the teacher's field audio and photo set.
  • Extension: look across every section and name a pattern. Post it as a comment on the section it connects to.

Using the Padlet ethically

  • Don't upload photos of people or of anything you were asked not to record.
  • Keep Woiwurrung words to those shared by Wurundjeri sources, and say where they came from.
  • Comment on the work, not the person. Every post is someone's experience of this place.

Lesson 4 · Notice

Designing with Country: Danièle Hromek

Djinjama viewing guideJigsaw groups
Learning intention
Analyse how a First Nations designer, Danièle Hromek, works with Country, and apply that lens to our archive.
Success criteria
  • I can identify and explain one principle of Hromek's practice.
  • I can re-read my archive through that lens and annotate what I missed.

Dr Danièle Hromek (Budawang/Dhurga/Yuin and Burrier/Dharawal) founded the design studio Djinjama. Open djinjama.com in a new tab.

Method, not knowledge. We are learning how Hromek works with Country. We are not borrowing Yuin knowledge or language for Wurundjeri Country. For example, Nura is a word for Country in Sydney-region languages, so we don't carry it into our own work.

Part 1: Jigsaw groups

Each group explores one Djinjama project from the Design page. Report back to the class.

  1. Listen at the threshold

    Read the Acknowledgement on the landing page aloud before entering the site. Why make visitors pause here?

  2. Notice the design

    List three visual choices. What does the layout put first?

  3. Find one principle

    Choose one value from the About page, such as "Always Country" or "Consume with conscience". Find evidence of it in your project. Who else shaped the design?

Part 2: Re-read the archive

Return to the Lesson 3 Padlet. Comment on your own posts in response to one question:

Where has design disregarded Country, or where could design happen with Country?

Annotate in words or visually (arrows, circles, overlays). Add one thing you missed the first time.

Supports

  • Jigsaw groups share the reading load.
  • Annotate visually if you prefer.
  • Extension reading: "Are you really Designing with Country?" (ArchitectureAU).

Think-pair-share: tell a partner the principle you chose and one pin you would re-read through it.

Lesson 5 · Make

Country as brief

Milestone 2: draft briefBrief template
Learning intention
Write a design brief in which Country's needs set the requirements.
Success criteria
  • My brief identifies context, needs, constraints and stakeholders.
  • It says whose knowledge it draws on and what I don't know.
  • It considers what Country might refuse, including removal or no intervention.

The task

Draft a brief for an object or intervention that adds to or removes something from Carran-carramulk. Your teacher will model a brief first.

Brief template

SectionSentence starter
ContextMy spot at Carran-carramulk is… Its layers include…
Country's needsThe river, plants and animals here need…
ConstraintsMy design must not… It must stay within…
StakeholdersThe people and more-than-human beings affected are…
Whose knowledgeMy brief draws on knowledge from… I don't know…
What Country might refuseCountry might not want… The option of removal or no intervention would mean…
ProposalI propose to add / remove… because…

Protocol: what we are permitted to make

Ours to makeAsk firstNot ours to make
Original responses to the place you observedWoiwurrung words, only from published Wurundjeri sources, creditedWurundjeri patterns, motifs or carving designs
Habitat, weed or litter interventionsAnything that names or tells a Wurundjeri story"Aboriginal-style" dot work or symbols
Wayfinding, signage, maps and labels in your own visual languageCollaborations with community groupsImages of Bunjil or other Ancestral beings
Sound pieces, posters, speculative proposalsPhotos of people at the siteTaking rocks, plants or bark from the site

Choose your format

  • Scaffolded: the template and sentence starters above.
  • Open: write your brief in your own structure, covering every section.
  • Visual brief: a moodboard with annotations for each section.

Your teacher will check in with you against the rubric. This draft begins your summative task.

← Lesson 4Lesson 6 →
Lesson 6 · Reflect

Critique circle

Milestone 3: revised brief and reflectionSummative
Learning intentions
Give and use feedback to make our briefs more ethical and culturally responsible.
Success criteria
  • I can give warm and cool feedback, including one ethics question.
  • I can revise my brief in response.
  • I can reflect on how my relationship to Country has shifted since Lesson 1.

The circle

  1. Present

    The maker shares their brief in one minute.

  2. Warm feedback

    "What works well is…"

  3. Cool feedback

    "I wonder whether… Could you…"

  4. One ethics question

    Every critique must ask one of these:

    Who benefits?
    Who was consulted?
    With Country, or for it?

  5. Revise

    Change at least one part of your brief in response.

Reflection: back to where you stand

Return to the place you mapped in Lesson 1. Write, record or draw a short reflection.

  1. In Lesson 1, I described my relationship to my place as…
  2. Since walking Carran-carramulk, I now think…
  3. One thing I chose not to design, and why…
  4. My responsibility to this place, and to mine, is…

Self-check

Supports

  • Feedback sentence prompts above.
  • Give critique in writing or out loud.
  • Small, stable groups if sharing is hard for you.
← Lesson 5About this unit →
For teachers and assessors

About this unit

A six-lesson Visual Communication Design unit for Years 9–10, located at Carran-carramulk (Dights Falls) on Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung Country. Students move from their own relationship to place, through a guided walk and a shared digital archive, to a design brief in which Country sets the requirements. Lesson 3 is the 30-minute digital lesson.

The river metaphor

The schema is drawn as the Birrarung below Merri Creek. The main channel is the lesson sequence, tributaries are access points, inputs from below are where Country, community and First Nations voices enter, and rings mark milestones. The river is a metaphor drawn from observing the site's waterways, not a First Nations framework.

The four phases

Student-facing phase names map onto the design process language of Visual Communication Design. The cycle repeats inside each lesson and across the whole unit.

ListenDiscover
NoticeDefine
MakeDevelop
ReflectDeliver

Cultural authority

Wurundjeri knowledge of the site comes from Wurundjeri voices, through the Wurundjeri Woi-wurrung Education Unit and Wurundjeri-approved sources. The name Carran-carramulk and any Woiwurrung words should be checked with the Education Unit before use.
